transcript:
The content of this podcast are for educational and entertainment purposes only and do not
perform to be in or out intended to be financial, legal, accounting, tax, or investment
advice.
Investments and strategies that are discussed may not be suitable for you.
Do not take no account in your particular investment objectives.
Financial situation or needs are not intended to provide investment advice or recommendations
appropriate for you.
Or make any investment trade, consider whether it's suitable for you and consider seeking
advice from your own financial or investment advisor.
It is such a great pleasure to have with us the one and only Monish Pabrai who truly
needs no introduction to the M.I. global community.
Very excited Monish that you are joining us after I believe two years.
We do this on a two year cycle.
There's a lot to discuss.
We got a ton of questions in from both M.O.I. members as well as the broader investment
community via X.
And so why don't we jump right in?
I think the most questions were actually around the coal industry, believe it or not.
So to the extent that you're willing to discuss would love to hear your thesis and feel
free to go as far back as you like, to sort of lay the foundation for how you became interested.
I mean, you know, we are still buyers in this space, so we don't need more competition
in terms of, you know, more people, quote, tailing, et cetera, but I can make some general
comments from a more from a mental model and education perspective.
And I think maybe your listeners may find this useful.
So just taking a step back a long time ago.
I think this must be close to 25 years ago, maybe 24, 25 years ago, Warren Buffett had
auctioned off his wallet.
And he had done a majority, I think it was a boy's town or something in Omaha.
And he had put a stock tip in the wallet.
And you know, that went for quite a bit of money, I don't remember how much.
But it turned out the stock tip was a company called First Industrial, which used to be
a REIT, an industrial REIT in Chicago.
And I was friends with the CEO of First Industrial, we were both in Chicago, so we knew each
other.
And I told him that, hey, by the way, you know, you know, that apparently Warren must
be a shareholder because he recommended you a stock.
And one of the things about REITs in general is that Berkshire Hathaway doesn't buy them
because the tax treatment is not friendly for corporations to own REITs.
So this was the case where he was probably buying it personally and there was no conflict
with Berkshire because Berkshire couldn't buy it even if it wanted to because it doesn't
work very well.
So I told him it's probably likely that Warren, personally, owns his shares, so he was intrigued
by that and he reached out to Warren and just said, you know, how humbled and grateful
he was that Warren would even have spent any time looking at his small business and Warren
responded to him saying that if you're ever in Omaha and don't call me, I will be quite
upset.
So then my friend basically told him, you know, what a coincidence.
I'm going to be in Omaha day after tomorrow.
So he went to Omaha, he and Warren had lunch, et cetera.
But one of the things that John had told me at around that time, I used to own First Industrial
Stock as well, is that he had mentioned that they mostly invested in industrial real estate
kind of warehouses and factories and that type of stuff.
And he said that the gestation period to build a warehouse usually is less than a year.
And he said the gestation period to build an office tower is maybe three to five years,
more like closer to five years with all the permissions and all of that.
He said that in industrial real estate, we don't get big cycles of booms and busts because
if there is tightness in the market and a lot of people go out and build a bunch of warehouses,
that space is going to hit the market in 12 months or 18 months.
And they may be, you know, some temporary weakness, but basically it would immediately,
if there was over building, it would reduce the propensity to build more warehouses.
And as the economy grew, that excess capacity would kind of get absorbed and things would
get to kind of baseline and again, when things got tight, people would build again.
But he said that in office towers because of the kind of five year period, when office
vacancies become very tight and rents go quite high, everyone and their brother starts
building towers at the same time.
And because of the three to five year gestation period, all these towers hit the market at
around the same time.
And the boom and bust cycles are much more pronounced because of this length and period.
Because basically, for example, if in 2020, we have a tightness in office towers, you
know, the first ones are going to get delivered in 2025.
So people will still be starting new office tower constructions in 21, 22, 23 and even
24 because they haven't seen the impact of all the inventory that's about to hit.
And you know, realistic guys are eternally optimistic till they get eternally pessimistic.
And of course, once that inventory hits, you've got more inventory coming for another
four or five years because of all the stuff that started.
So basically, you would have a five year boom, followed by a five to ten year bust and
then the cycle repeats.
So he says that the boom and bust cycles get kind of aggravated in the case of office towers.
And in fact, in Austin where I live right now, we are seeing that layout right now with
tall residential towers, kind of luxury residential towers.
I mean, Austin was going through so much growth, you know, three, four years ago that real
estate was very tight and difficult to get a space and all that and pretty much everyone
started building.
And now these big towers are being completed.
Some of them are going to be completed in the next one or two years and there's a huge
glut and such.
So it's not just office towers.
We see that even in residential towers because the same kind of phenomena, but this particular
notion of the gestation period and boom and bust how pronounced it is.
What I found instead time and I spoke to John about this is that it comes up in many
other sectors and I noticed the same thing around outside like 22 years ago in the oil
shipping business, you know, the very large crude carriers.
And again, this was the situation I think in maybe 2001 or so when there are about 400
of these VLCCs, very large crude carriers that are used to carry larger amounts of crude
around the world and there was a big glut.
I mean, basically oil demand went down and there were too many tankers.
And because there were too many tankers, rental rates collapsed and these tankers were
being rented out below, they were rented at a loss basically because it was better than
making zero.
You know, if you got, if your cost was 15 or 20,000 dollars a day, from one of these VLCCs,
the rates went down as low as 708,000 and what happened at that time was that there was
a lot of scrapping because you know, these owners were so distressed.
The global fleet went from like 400 to 360 or 350 with a lot of scrapping because these
owners wanted to get some cash.
And then the market tightened oil demand came back, but the tankers had the exact same
situation as the office towers, they take again three, four years to get delivered after
you place an order with the Korean shipyards.
And also the second thing that happens is that when there's a boom, so what happened
is these oil tanker rates went to like 7,000 a day, they went all the way to a quarter
million dollars a day.
I mean, they went to the other extreme.
It was just extreme obscene profitability for these tanker companies.
And everyone and their brother at that time went to the Korean shipyards and placed orders.
And of course, the Koreans are not stupid.
They know that they are the toll bridge that everyone has to pass through to get their
tankers.
Prices for new build tankers went through the roof like what used to be every million
dollars ship might be quoted at 120 million, 130 million, 150 million, because what are
you going to do?
You want a ship?
You pay what the guy wants to charge you.
And of course, the problem is that when those ships got delivered, again, they all hit
at the same time and then, you know, the same cycle.
So what I've noticed in the last two and a half decades is this mental model, which applies
to office towers, as actually applies to many different classes of investments and actually
understanding that mental model can give you a big edge.
And one of the things in the cold space, especially the metallurgical cold space, which is
a cold that's used to make iron and steel, is that coal is now a full-lettered world.
So I remember I was talking to one of the cold seers in the Appalachians.
And this is not a medical company, this is a thermal cold company, I think a console
energy, which now just merged with art and has become core natural resources.
And console is 150 year old thermal coal company, very, very high quality thermal coal, extremely
low cost operation.
In 150 years of operating because of their strong product quality and low prices, they've
never had financial distress, they've never gone bankrupt, which is almost an anomaly
in mining.
In 150 years, console never had to restructure, never went bankrupt, nothing because they
were always at the bottom of the end of the cost curve, and they always had the highest
quality coal.
And so they always made money, literally they would be the last mines to shut down.
And the console in your management was telling me that they've had banking relationship
with JP Morgan Chase for maybe several decades, might be 50, 60, 70 years.
And JP Morgan told them that they can no longer have them as a client.
Now console is not borrowing any money, they have two or three billion in revenue.
And so if you're a commercial bank banker of someone like console, with all their letters
of credit and all the cash flowing through the account, it's a highly, highly profitable
account.
Or a JP Morgan to come and tell them that they couldn't have them as a client because
they were pretty much a ideal client was just because of ESG pressures.
And these ESG pressures have gotten very irrational.
So console, for example, has difficulty getting workers' comp insurance.
Now the company is very willing and does self-insured for millions of dollars per incident or per
worker.
So they actually don't need the insurance, they're effectively self-insured.
They just need insurance to satisfy the statutory requirement that they have workers' comp insurance.
And so the insurance company is never going to see a claim.
But again, the same thing, because of ESG pressures, they have a lot of difficulty getting
courts, they have a lot of difficulty getting shorty companies to give them courts.
So literally all the kind of factors of production that they need to run their business, treat
them like a pariah.
And especially historically mining companies, they needed to raise debt in addition to equity
whenever they were going to have some kind of capex or growth or whatever.
If a JP Morgan is not allowed, you know, interested in having you as a banking client who's never
borrowing money, they're definitely not going to have you as a client that they don't lend
money to.
And so these coal companies basically had two things happen to them which were very unusual
for the mining business.
The first is because of the Ukraine war and the super normal pricing for coal in 2022,
all of them were debt-free.
They paid off every last bit of debt, which was never the case.
You know, coal companies, mining companies always had debt.
And that's what would usually get them into trouble is because prices would go down, they'd
be a down cycle, they couldn't service the debt, they would go bankrupt and then the cycle
would repeat and so on.
But we had this situation starting in 2022 and 23 where a lot of the coal businesses
were net cash, which has never been net cash.
And not only were they net cash, the second issue is the same boom and bust mental model
applies here as well.
So let's say for example, there's a downturn in the metallurgical coal market where prices
are too low.
It's losing money or barely making money.
Well, what would happen is that the high-cost mines eventually would shut down because they
would try to run them for some time, even at a loss because they'd be hoping for a turn.
But at some point if this persisted long enough, they would shut down.
In fact, we currently have weak pricing for metallurgical coal and a number of appellation
mines and mines around the world have shut down.
And now when these mines shut down, restart is very complicated.
So let's say for example, you know, metallurgical coal prices right now, PLV, the Australian
index, let's say it's 190 or 200 or ton currently, which is quite low and a lot of producers
would have difficulty making ends meet at that price.
Let's say for example, the price went to 300, 250 or 300, well, that would make it
very profitable for a lot of a lot of mines, including the mines that have recently shut
down.
But if those same companies or individuals tried to restart those mines, they would face
a lot of difficulties.
So typically when you shut down a coal mine, what happens is that you lay off all the miners
and you sell off all the equipment, you pull all the equipment out and you sell it off
because what are you going to do with it?
I mean, you want to raise as much money as you can and salvage whatever you can.
So the equipment is gone.
The workers are gone and sometimes the mining permit is gone because you've got to keep
paying royalties and different taxes, etc.
So the permit when we gone as well.
Now when you want to do a restart, the first issue you're going to face is there's no
financing available.
So any restart would need to be kind of all equity restarts, which is unusual in mining.
Even if you could arrange the money on a pure equity basis, the difficulty with raising
money on a pure equity basis, to start a mine where all prices are high, is there's no
assurance of what the coal price is going to be six months, one year, two years or three
years from now.
So what type of risk capital is willing to be willing to come in equity or debt when
the future is unknown, you know, the three hundred dollar price might last for three weeks
or three years.
We don't know.
And so first is the financing debt or equity will be problematic.
If that hurdle was crossed, when the index prices go high, there are no miners available
and it takes years and years and years to build those skills.
So it's not like you can go place and add and hire miners.
So when you've gotten rid of your miners and they've gone, taken other jobs, gone
to other industries or whatever else, trying to get miners back or get higher miners in a
three hundred dollar per ton environment would be very challenging.
So that'd be the second barrier to entry.
The third barrier to entry would be that when you try to procure the equipment, just like
the Korean shipyards, the equipment is going to be two to four year backlogs, two three
four year backlogs.
And just like the Korean shipyards, you would be paying very high prices for the equipment
because the equipment manufacturers are in the driver's seat.
So you would face a multi-year period to get the equipment, a lot of challenges to get
the labor, a lot of challenges to get the capital.
And then even the permits may become difficult depending on the geographies and such
because coal is the four lettered word.
So unlike office towers, where there's some predictability and such that, you know, your
main kind of gating factor would be, is someone willing to lend to you.
And if rents are high, they may be banks willing to do that.
They may even be people willing to sign leases with you in the future, etc.
So coal has this situation, I think, with the boom and bust.
That is, I think more intense now than with a lot of the other situations.
We see this boom and bust situation, not just in office towers or residential towers or
coal, we see it in many, many places.
So for example, if we were to look today at offshore oil drilling rigs, which when
through a period of severe distress a few years ago, and again, they have the same situation
three, two, four, four years to build a rig.
And these rigs cost a billion, billion and a half.
And again, currently there is an oversupply.
So no one's going to build a rig when there's no supply.
But you know, when it gets typed, again, you've got a three, four, five year period.
I think from an education perspective for the MOI global community and your listeners
at large, I think that I have found in my investing career a focus on this mental model
to be very lucrative.
And once you understand this mental model, and you're able to go long in one of these
areas at the right time in the cycle.
What can happen on the other end can challenge your wildest imagination.
So the the booms can be very spectacular.
So what I find with some of our coal bets is they have no debt.
They've got a very good position on the cost curve.
And you know, we kind of break even or maybe lose a little bit of money at the low end.
But when we've got super normal profits coming at the other end, so that's a good equation
for my perspective.
Well, thank you so much, Monish.
That really is very educational and can be applied as you say to many different industries
at different points in time.
It sounds like capital cycle theory on steroids right now for coal and maybe for offshore
drillers as well.
Or some even say, you know, if you take copper miners, it takes like a decade or something
like that to bring a new copper mine online.
And in something like copper, you have the long term tailwind also of greater electricity
and so forth.
Maybe wondering, you know, if that's the thesis, why not also expose yourself to a few
other industries that have that same thesis as kind of a risk management tool?
I'm always open.
I like that model.
But I think that it's not enough to just understand that a particular industry has the
booms and bus.
You also have to have some other ingredients in place, you know, the right management team,
the right capital structure, typically you would be coming into these industries at
times when things may not be, I mean, they will not be at a boom.
They may not be at the absolute bottom, but they may be somewhere between the bottom and
the boom.
And so you typically would be entering at a time of merceness.
And so being able to, for the entity to have the resilience to live, to see the boom
and fully capitalize on it will vary from a business to business.
So one would need to evaluate that.
But yeah, absolutely, it applies in many different contexts.
And so it sounds like that is another kind of pattern or pattern recognition comes in,
comes with experience also as you said with the tankers, I remember probably a couple
decades ago or more when you invested in those when they were trading for less than scrap.
So how do you kind of take that and also the other side which is investing in great businesses
for the long term, I know you do both.
How do you trade one off versus the other?
The tanker bet was quite profitable, but it was extremely painful.
And I just want to explain that a little bit before I answer the rest of your question.
Basically I had done at that time only first order thinking.
I had not done second order thinking with the tankers.
So it was very clear to me when I made the investment in front line tankers of ELCCs that
all their debt was non-recourse.
The debt was at the individual tanker level.
And the parent had almost no debt.
And there was a ready market for these tankers to be traded, there's a market for them
to be scrapped, et cetera.
And when you looked at the market cap and the debt and you looked at just kind of liquidation
value of the portfolio, there was no way you could lose money.
I mean, the market cap was so much below liquidation that.
So I didn't even pay a lot of attention to the upside.
I just knew that from a downside perspective, it was very protected.
And it was a relatively easy 50, 70, 80% return in maybe not that much time.
And in fact, I think in less than a year, maybe even less than six months, we had like
a 70, 80% return.
And I sold our position.
And I patterned myself on the back saying, well done, Monish.
And then completely missed what happened after that.
So I think if I had held on to front line for the next few years because things went
to stable, the rental rates went to 20, 25,000, which means they were profitable, the stock
moved up.
And then it went all the way to $253,000 a day.
And at that point, I mean, it's ungodly cash flows coming into the business because their
entire fleet was on the spot market.
And what I did not appreciate then is John Fedrickson, who was the German and CEO, was a gifted
capital allocator, I mean, just an incredible operator.
And so it would have been, I think when I calculated in about four or five years, a 70-bagger
investment for us instead it wasn't even a double.
And that was terrible.
And so it got seared into me.
And so one of the things to understand is these things don't go into nice buckets where
you can say that Google is a great business and the oil tankers are just a special situation.
It's not quite true exactly.
I mean, I think that oil tanker business was one could have just done some second order
thinking and understood that there were some possibilities, some non-zero possibilities
that there was some spectacular result possibilities if one just hung on for a little bit.
So I think in investing, flexibility is important.
I think I always like to say that Warren Buffett has a kind of a Swiss army knife in his
pocket when he goes by doing his investments.
And for example, when Berkshire made their investment in the Japanese trading companies,
I mean, they borrowed almost the entire amount.
This is the company that has its drowning in cash, you know, 100 billion plus in cash.
And he still borrows the amount for the entire investment in yen because mathematically,
it was the right thing to do.
I mean, it was just an infinite return on equity that he got on that investment is truly
spectacular.
So I think in investing, obviously, the best place to be is the great businesses that
are bought at great prices that are going to execute well for a very long time.
And you're going to end up with 10, 20, 30, 50, 100 times your money in some 10, 20 years
or whatever.
That's ideal.
But some of these other things that are, which might be categorized as special situations
can also be, you know, the lines of blur.
It's not very clear red line or black line that one's on one side and one's on the other.
So flexibility is important and being open is important.
And I believe there was a little bit also the thesis with micron when you first came
across it because that industry had been basically a bad, commoditized industry for a
long time.
And you saw that that was changing.
So would you say that was also a little bit along those lines?
Yeah.
I mean, micron was an oligopoly, the three players.
The barriers to entry are extremely high.
I mean, it's almost impossible for any, even if you gave somebody a hundred billion dollars
to enter the memory business.
I think it, in fact, I think the CFO, I think the one time CFO of micron, I think the
micron had told me once that there is so much black magic involved in the production of
memory chips that he said that if one of their fabs burnt down and they've got all the
patterns and they've got everything, they aren't sure that they can get a replacement fab
up and running.
Even though theoretically they know how to make memory because there is so much kind of
black magic type stuff in the production of memory, the yields and all that.
So it's a difficult, it's a very difficult business.
And so yeah, if you've got three players and they're rational actors and they're likely
to be rational actors, then that would likely work out well.
And I think on micron bed worked okay, I mean, in the sense that I think what happened
is I think we had a double in a few years.
But then other stuff showed up on the radar that looked just far more interesting.
And so I made the switch and moved on.
But yeah, micron, especially now when we see everything that's happening with the eye
and all that, I mean, the memory guys are a good place to be.
And another thing, another example I believe a couple of years ago you looked at Meta and
said that it was an easy double which it has been even more than that.
And there's a compounder that got really cheap.
So given how many great ideas you find, how do you think about portfolio concentration
and how many ideas to own at any given time because it seems like some of these ideas could
be owned in parallel instead of focusing on one or the other?
Yeah, I think Meta was a good case.
It looked cheap.
It's a good business.
You know, a number of the businesses inside Meta are products that we all use on a daily
basis.
So a lot of people would have competence and understanding of what Meta's business is.
I actually never invested in Meta even though I saw that.
And probably one of my flaws and mental blocks is I have difficulty with the mega caps.
You know, just kind of the law of large numbers is something is really big.
Well, how much more bigger can it get?
Like, you know, if you make an investment in Nvidia or Microsoft or Apple, you know, multi
trillion dollar market caps, you know, where is it 10 or 20 years from now?
And someone like me would be skeptical and sometimes I'd be wrong about that.
So for whatever reason at that time, I didn't go for Meta because of this concern and probably
because there were other names on the radar that looked interesting.
I don't know whether they performed as well or not, but that's just the way it rolls.
What I try to do in portfolio is typically the 10 by 10, where if I'm making a bet, I'd
make it 10% of the portfolio.
Now, what ends up happening is that if you get a very big winner in one of those bets,
then the portfolio will start to get skewed.
And I see different degrees of skewing in some of the different portfolios I run.
So for example, we have an offshore fund and an offshore hedge fund.
And it has, you know, 400 odd million in assets.
